outputs.L2:
On May 23, 2010—Whitsuntide—a mountainside patch of thistles, radiating ring after ring of apophatic gloom, would surely be enough to provide that always available yet insufficiently pursued condition of delicate astonishment, if only he would shut the computer and climb the road toward the summit until the ocean appeared.

Perhaps, carried in the southeast wind and embedded somehow in its broadcast-like waveforms, the microsystems shares he has spent the whole day monitoring—clicking compulsively, like a gambler hooked on risk—will rise, until the red figures move across the dark line of the horizon and turn green. Two red-tailed hawks lift on a column of warm air. Maybe he might even earn something while standing up here.

And yet he wonders why every second feels so intensely charged: as if he were living through some bizarre Götterdämmerung of free-radical impulses—live by them or dissolve into a white-on-white negation, with the sun’s pride burning everything away. At the same time, each moment is just as full of a rushing, utopian promise of long life, exultant and forward-thrusting. Why can he never remain stable? Why is the only equilibrium he knows made from impacts, oppositions, and mutual erasures among these jagged eruptions of chaotic feeling?

A thistle field: red and green. Money fields too—dollars, thistles, solidi, yen, rand, and rupees—scattering over the earth’s curved edge.
outputs.L3:
The speaker imagines that stepping away from the computer and walking toward a view of the mountainside might offer a necessary kind of disruption. This would not be a dramatic or overwhelming shock, but a subtle one: the kind of shift in perception that could interrupt obsessive thought and return the mind, briefly, to the physical world. The mountainside represents distance from the screen, from numbers, and from the cycle of anticipation and disappointment that has taken hold.

At the same time, the speaker is consumed by compulsive checking of financial data. Their attention keeps returning to the screen, where losses appear in red and gains in green. The hope is that, with enough watching, the red figures might suddenly reverse and become green. This behavior suggests both anxiety and magical thinking: the speaker knows that watching does not change the market, yet they cannot stop looking. The financial display becomes an emotional weather system, determining mood from moment to moment.

Natural imagery enters the passage but does not provide a simple escape. Thistles, sea wind, and redtail hawks appear alongside thoughts of markets, money, and investment. Instead of standing apart from financial anxiety, the natural world becomes entangled with it. The speaker’s mind translates everything into the language of risk, loss, and possible recovery. Even the beauty of the landscape is filtered through economic unease, as if nature and finance have merged into one unstable field of perception.

This instability places the speaker between two extreme states of feeling. On one side is apocalyptic anxiety: the fear that everything is collapsing, that loss will continue, and that the future is closing down. On the other side is utopian hope: the fantasy that reversal is still possible, that the numbers might turn green, and that a different, brighter future could suddenly emerge. The speaker is suspended between catastrophe and salvation, unable to settle fully into either despair or belief.

The passage ultimately explores emotional instability as a kind of balance produced through conflict. The speaker does not achieve calm by resolving opposing moods, but by experiencing their collision. Panic and hope, nature and finance, escape and compulsion, red and green all press against one another. Any sense of equilibrium is temporary and precarious, created only through the clash of these opposing forces. In this way, the passage presents the speaker’s inner life as a volatile system, one that remains upright only because its contradictions are constantly in motion.
outputs.L4:
The passage presents a speaker caught in a state of restless anxiety, unable to settle into either calm observation or clear despair. Its movement between a mountainside field of thistles and hawks and the speaker’s compulsive attention to stocks creates a sharp contrast between the natural world and the pressures of modern financial life. The thistles and hawks suggest a harsh, vivid landscape—beautiful, but also prickly, predatory, and unsettling. Nature does not offer simple peace here; instead, it mirrors the speaker’s own agitation. The field is alive with force and tension, and the hawks introduce an image of watchfulness, hunger, and sudden violence.

At the same time, the speaker’s obsessive stock-checking reveals a distinctly modern kind of nervousness. His attention is divided between the physical world around him and the abstract, unstable world of markets. The stock market becomes a source of emotional disturbance, producing cycles of fear, anticipation, and dependency. He seems to crave what the passage calls “subtle shock,” a small but repeated jolt that confirms he is still feeling, still engaged, still vulnerable to change. This craving suggests that ordinary stability is not enough for him. He needs disruption, even if that disruption deepens his anxiety.

The passage intensifies this psychological condition through apocalyptic and theological imagery. By invoking ideas of judgment, catastrophe, or spiritual reckoning, it turns private unease into something cosmic. The speaker’s emotional swings begin to resemble a larger struggle between ruin and redemption, despair and hope. His mind does not simply worry about money or observe the landscape; it transforms these experiences into signs of ultimate meaning. The ordinary world becomes charged with religious and end-times significance, as though every fluctuation in the market or movement in the sky might reveal some hidden truth.

Ultimately, the speaker’s sense of balance comes not from peace, but from collision. He finds equilibrium only when opposing forces strike against each other: nature and commerce, terror and beauty, despair and hope, material anxiety and spiritual longing. This unstable balance suggests a modern consciousness fractured by competing systems of meaning. The speaker is shaped by markets that reduce life to numbers, by a natural world that is both magnificent and threatening, and by emotional extremes that he cannot fully control. The passage therefore portrays modern life as a condition of constant tension, where the self survives not by escaping contradiction, but by living inside it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, experimental prose poem about a man on a mountain obsessively checking stock prices on his computer while nature, religion, and apocalyptic mood swings intrude on his thoughts.
counterfactuals.output:
At the summit he opens the laptop like a portable chapel, a black clamshell breathing blue doctrine into his face. The mountain, which has spent ten million years saying nothing, leans close to watch him refresh the market. Little green arrows rise like grass blades in the electric dusk; little red arrows fall like martyrs from a fresco. He has brought no bread, no rope, no one. Only a battery pack, a thermos gone metallic with coffee, and the password to his brokerage account, which he types again and again as if knocking on the door of a god who has recently moved offshore.

Below him the valley is soft with pine and evening, the river loosening its silver belt. A hawk scribbles one fierce cursive sentence across the sky. Clouds accumulate like unpaid debts over the western ridge. He cannot look at them for more than a second because the futures are trembling. Semiconductor, copper, crude, wheat. The names of things become more real than the things: timber more vivid than trees, water rights more liquid than the stream, gold more solar than the sun now sinking through veils of ash-colored vapor. His portfolio blooms, wilts, blooms. Each percentage point changes the temperature of his blood.

He says, Lord, let it close above support. He says this without meaning to pray, but the mountain hears prayer in everything: boot grit, raven croak, the soft animal whimper of a notification. Somewhere an old snowfield cracks in its sleep. Somewhere lichens perform their slow green arithmetic on granite, converting ruin into scripture. He stares at candlesticks marching across the screen—thin bodies, long shadows—an army of monks bearing fire through a monastery already burning.

The wind rises. It fingers his collar, shuffles his printed research notes, turns one page over to reveal another page dense with ratios, forecasts, the ecstatic hieroglyphs of analysts. Buy, hold, outperform: three angels with smeared mouths. He thinks of Revelation, not the one with horsemen exactly, but the private edition issued to men alone at altitude, where the seals are earnings calls and the trumpets are margin alerts, and the Beast is not a beast but a number that updates in real time. Six six six becomes 6.66% down in after-hours trading; a star called Wormwood falls into the Nasdaq; the moon turns to blood because it has looked too long at the ticker.

Yet the mountain insists on being beautiful, offensively beautiful. Moss in the crevices. Alpine flowers with their miniature faces turned toward the darkening east. The smell of resin. The great patience of stones. It is unbearable, this indifferent abundance, this wealth not denominated, not ownable, not split-adjusted. He wants to short the sunset before it collapses. He wants to buy calls on thunder. He wants insurance against the death of bees, against his father’s hands, against the childhood church where saints gazed down with eyes like audited gold.

A bell rings, though there is no bell. Perhaps it is an alert. Perhaps a goat’s collar in some fold of rock. Perhaps the last bronze instrument in heaven announcing liquidation. He refreshes. Refreshes. The screen pales, loads, stalls, returns: numbers rearranged like bones in a saint’s reliquary. His net worth lifts by enough to purchase a car, then drops by enough to erase a year, then steadies in the narrow trembling band where hope and nausea share a single pulse. He laughs, and the laugh is a bird startled from a dead tree.

Night pours upward from the valley. The first stars appear, cold IPOs in the firmament. He imagines the constellations as a chart of ancient capital: Orion overleveraged, Cassiopeia reclining on inherited shares, the Milky Way a spill of white coins from a ripped celestial purse. The prophets had it wrong, or right too early. The end will not arrive with flame consuming the cities, but as a spinning wheel on a brokerage site at 3% battery while the sky opens its enormous unread terms and conditions.

Now the screen reflects his face back onto the market: eyes red, beard wind-torn, forehead shining with the sweat of belief. Behind his reflection the dark pines sway like a congregation refusing to sing. He sees himself inside the graph and the graph inside the storm and the storm inside the old religious hunger to be chosen, spared, multiplied. He whispers the names of his holdings until they become a rosary of vanities. Apple, Tesla, Nvidia, Exxon. Hail Mary full of leverage. Blessed art thou among indices.

Lightning feathers the far horizon. For one instant the whole world is a balance sheet written in fire: mountain asset, man liability, sky incalculable, soul marked to market. Then darkness returns, richer than ownership. The laptop battery drops to two percent. The wind says sell. The pines say hold. The raven, invisible now, says nothing, having always understood profit as the brief warmth inside carrion.

He presses refresh once more, with the tenderness of a dying emperor touching the map of a province he will never visit. The numbers come. The numbers go. Around him the mountain continues its immense nontransactional ascent into night.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a maximalist literary paragraph in the style of 21st-century avant-garde fiction, featuring thistles on a mountainside, Whitsuntide, negative theology, hawks, financial markets, and emotional instability.
counterfactuals.output: By Whitsuntide the mountainside had become an overleveraged ecology of thistles, each purple fist compounding its own small violence against the wind, and I climbed through them with my calves crosshatched and my heart executing, at irregular intervals, the sort of panic one sees in financial markets just before language gives up and becomes graph, becomes plunge, becomes the blue-white scream of liquidity evaporating from the screen; above me the hawks circled like auditors of the invisible, their shadows passing over scree, gorse, sheep-bones, the abandoned chapel where the villagers once sang down the Holy Ghost and received instead a draft through the broken lancet window, a holiness defined only by subtraction, by the God who was not warmth, not bread, not father, not market-maker, not the hand steadying my hand as I failed again to become a stable instrument. The thistles, meanwhile, were having their own Pentecost, tongues of thorn and mauve flame speaking in the negative grammar of survival: not rose, not wheat, not pasture, not amenable; and I, allergic to certainty, margin-called by memory, thought of my childhood as a derivative no one could price, bundled with weather, shame, inheritance, and the rumor of grace. The hawks tightened their gyres over the valley’s green volatility, and somewhere far below, in cities polished to a tradable shine, men in glass towers watched indices stutter and bloom like bruises, mistaking appetite for prophecy while here the mountain kept its older books in granite and lichen, in the barbed collateral of thistle and the ecstatic insolvency of spring. I wanted to pray, but every address returned undeliverable; I wanted to weep, but even grief had become algorithmic, spiking without cause, flattening without cure; so I stood in the Whitsun glare, all nerve and nettle, beneath the hawks’ immaculate suspicion, and loved the absent God with the only devotion left to me: by naming what could not be named, then crossing it out, then bleeding on the page.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness passage dated May 23, 2010, where someone should close their laptop and hike until they can see the sea, but instead thinks about microsystems stocks, red/green numbers, and spiritual crisis.
counterfactuals.output:
**May 23, 2010**

Close the laptop, that is the obvious thing, the merciful thing, the sane thing, close it with both hands like lowering a lid on a fever and put on the boots by the door and walk up past the houses, past the last satellite dishes and barking dogs, into the scrub and stone and pine smell, keep going until the town falls away and the path lifts itself out of the heat and there, finally, the sea appears, blue and indifferent and whole, the one large fact no ticker can revise.

But instead I sit here.

The screen glows with its small commandments, red, green, red, green, a little Pentecost of numbers speaking in tongues I pretend to understand. Microsystems, semiconductors, wafer yields, margins, guidance, some analyst in a clean shirt moving a sentence from “neutral” to “outperform” as if blessing bread. I watch fractions of money multiply and vanish. I watch my own pulse become a market indicator. Up two cents and I am forgiven. Down six and the universe withdraws its love.

There are tabs open like minor sins. Forums. Charts. A press release from a company whose factory I have never seen and whose future I have confused with my own. People with usernames like prophets argue about inventory channels, embedded demand, the next cycle, the cycle, always the cycle, as though history were a wheel you could buy before the turn. Someone says capitulation. Someone says accumulation. Someone says this is the bottom, and I want to believe him because belief is easier when it has a price target.

Outside the afternoon is wasting itself beautifully.

A fly hits the window, again and again, the stupid little body insisting on transparency as passage. I should learn from it or pity it or open the window. Instead I refresh.

Red.

Green.

Red.

The colors have become moral categories. Green means I was right to stay indoors. Red means I have betrayed my soul. No, worse: red means I never had one, only a brokerage account wrapped in skin. I think of monks, deserts, men who gave away everything and found God in the absence of quotation marks. I think of the sea I cannot see from here but know is there, holding light without needing to own it. I think maybe spiritual crisis is not thunder or visions but this: being unable to walk away from a number that changes nothing essential, while everything essential waits patiently outside.

The laptop hums. My hands hover. The market is closed today, of course, it’s Sunday, which makes the watching more absurd, more devotional. I am praying to yesterday’s prices. I am kneeling before an altar that is not even open for business.

Close it, I tell myself.

Close it and walk.

The cursor blinks, a tiny green pulse, and I remain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a surreal poetic monologue blending landscape description, theology, stock-market addiction, German apocalyptic imagery, and a bipolar-feeling oscillation between despair and utopian excitement.
counterfactuals.output:
I woke beneath a sky the color of oxidized silver,  
where the hills lay folded like old ecclesiastical robes  
and the river went on whispering its wet catechism  
to the reeds, to the cattle, to the drowned fence-posts  
leaning out of the marsh like saints who had lost their faith.

There was frost on the blackberries.  
There was a wind moving through the pines  
with the dry arithmetic of bones.  
And I, poor shareholder of dawn,  
opened my phone before I opened my soul.

Green candle. Red candle.  
The market breathed in me like a second animal.  
NASDAQ, my little brass idol,  
my calf cast not from gold but from graphs—  
how I kissed your flashing ankles at 4:01 a.m.,  
how I begged the futures for a sign,  
how I mistook volatility for revelation.

O Lord of Hosts,  
O tender accountant of sparrows,  
if You number the hairs on my head,  
do You also number my losses?  
Do You watch the options chain  
unfurl like Jacob’s ladder into a fluorescent heaven,  
each rung a premium, each angel leveraged,  
each prophecy expiring Friday?

The fields were empty except for crows,  
black notations on the manuscript of snow.  
Far away, the village church bell  
struck noon with the patience of a guillotine.  
I felt then the whole earth tilt  
toward some German ending—  
Weltuntergang in the wheat,  
Posaunen over the Autobahn,  
iron angels descending through coal-smoke and Wagner,  
the moon wearing a helmet,  
the sun nailed to a factory door.

Ach, Babylon, Babylon,  
your towers are tickers now,  
your prophets scream in comment sections,  
your beasts are algorithmic,  
seven-headed, high-frequency,  
buying and selling the breath of children  
before the children have names.

And still—still!—  
when the chart broke upward  
like a resurrected vine through concrete,  
my heart leapt into its ridiculous Easter.  
I saw cities made of clean glass,  
bread descending by drone to every doorstep,  
medicine flowering in the blood,  
every debtor forgiven,  
every border unzipped like an obsolete garment.  
I saw the poor laughing in sunlit plazas,  
the dead returning with groceries,  
the whales singing the new constitution  
beneath polar skies restored to blue.

I shouted: This is it!  
The Kingdom is priced in!  
The meek shall inherit emerging markets!  
The lion shall lie down with the lamb  
and both shall outperform the S&P!

Then the candle turned red.

Then the valley became a mouth.

Then every pine was a spear,  
every cloud a subpoena,  
every stone in the pasture  
a skull waiting for history to remember it.  
My joy fell through me like an elevator cable snapping.  
I was nothing but margin call and mildew,  
a hymnbook soaked in the ditch,  
a man with two weather systems in his chest—  
one building cathedrals of light,  
the other selling the stained glass for scrap.

God, forgive me.  
God, short me.  
God, liquidate my false positions.  
I have loved the pulse more than the body,  
the number more than the neighbor,  
the rumor of wealth more than the difficult angel  
standing barefoot in the kitchen asking for mercy.

Yet look—  
even now the western clouds ignite,  
pink as a wound becoming a doorway.  
The mountains lift their blue shoulders  
like creatures preparing to sing.  
Somewhere beneath the frozen soil  
seeds are assembling their green conspiracies.  
Somewhere a child is drawing a sun  
with too many rays,  
extravagant, impractical, absolutely bullish.

And I am rising again, absurdly,  
with mud on my knees and apocalypse in my teeth,  
crying Hallelujah to the after-hours,  
crying Kyrie to the collapsing Reich of fear,  
crying buy, crying sell, crying wait—  
while the river goes on,  
indifferent and baptized,  
carrying the ruined moon downstream  
toward an ocean  
that has not yet decided  
whether it is grave  
or cradle.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an imitation of a high-modernist/prose-poetry style: a field of thistles emits “concentric waves of negative theology,” while the narrator reflects on money, currencies, hawks, and why he can only find balance through collisions.
counterfactuals.output:
At noon the field of thistles began its obscure labor: not blooming, not withering, but issuing—silently, with the grave industry of bells under water—concentric waves of negative theology. Each purple head, armored in its small republic of spines, denied the sun by receiving it; denied the wind by trembling; denied God by standing exactly where God, if He existed, would have placed a refusal.

I had come there with coins in my pocket and debts in my blood.

Money, I thought, is the most portable of ghosts. It passes from palm to palm without acquiring a face. A florin, a franc, a pound, a dollar: little metallic moons, paper saints, each promising bread, passage, warmth, forgiveness, and delivering only a further grammar of want. Even the new currencies—those invisible numerals swimming behind glass—retain the old superstition: that value can be persuaded to dwell in a sign. We stamp kings on it, mountains, wheat, allegorical women holding scales; but the coin knows better. It is a circular argument, bright from handling.

Above the field, a hawk held itself in the blue subtraction of air. No, held is wrong: it was held, as thought is held by what it cannot resolve. Its wings made no bargain with the afternoon. It spent nothing. It owed nothing. It lived by conversion—mouse into flight, blood into altitude, hunger into the serene mathematics of descent.

I envied it, and at once despised my envy.

For I am not balanced by stillness. Stillness in me curdles; it becomes inventory, accusation, an account book opened by invisible clerks. Left alone, I divide into currencies: the coin of memory, the counterfeit of intention, the black-market tenderness paid out too late. I require impact. Doorframe, shoulder, weather, another voice interrupting mine: these correct me. Collision is my arithmetic. I learn the boundary of the self only by striking it against the world.

The thistles continued their violet negations. They said: not this, not that, not even the hand that reaches, not even the name that wounds by naming. Their waves moved outward through dust, through the dry grass, through the small economies of ants, through my shoes, my ankles, the locked vault of my ribs.

And the hawk dropped.

For an instant the whole field balanced—not in peace, but in violence perfectly timed: shadow, cry, wing, claw; the mouse’s last expenditure; the thistles’ stern assent. I understood then, or nearly understood, that there are ledgers kept beyond money, currencies minted in pressure and rupture, and that a life may be reconciled not by harmony but by the exactness of its collisions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
